title: After the concert: radio show, Nixon's Grand and the musicians who worked for him
summary: The concert ran until 2 p.m. next day. Rose then hired halls and hosted WFIL's Journeys into Jazz. He met Danny Barker and Red Allen at Nixon's Grand and booked many Chicago and New York players.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: And, uh, the people were extremely enthusiastic and they didn't get out of the concert until two o'clock the next afternoon. In broad daylight. The next afternoon. That's right. Mm-hmm. We started at eight o'clock at night and kept on until two o'clock the next afternoon, which may also be a marathon record for jazz concerts. So, anyway, uh, after that, uh, I was widely congratulated and people, uh, were saying, well, you know, we gotta do this again. And then I took to, uh, to, uh, hiring small halls, uh, for small groups of people and, and arranging with the musicians to come in and play. Then I was approached by, uh, the radio station there, WFIL, uh, which was the ABC affiliate at the time. And they asked me if I would come in and do a regular record show, uh, based on this kind of music. And, uh, I did, entitled Journeys into Jazz, uh, which still runs on tape in various parts of the country at various times. And, uh, so, uh, people began to identify me with the music. And having done so, of course, the musicians that I was associated with then would let me know what was happening and who was available and because jobs were scarce in those days. Now, it also happened that the university was right across the street from a theater, which was called Nixon's Grand Theater, where most of the, uh, black musical attractions played. And so, uh, and of course, a lot of the members of those bands were New Orleans musicians, some of whom I knew from New Orleans. And some of whom, uh, uh, were referred to me by other people, by other musicians.

You see, in New York. Who knew them? So I used to take to going across the street whenever a new band came in and saying hello and finding out who was going to be doing what and if there was a possibility I might be able to use them on a concert.

And, uh, this is how I met people like Danny Barker, for instance. Uh-huh. Even though I had seen him performing in New Orleans when I was a kid, I didn't know his name and I didn't identify the name with the person until I met him in backstage at Nixon's Grand and Red Allen and people like that.
Did you have, in producing these concerts, did you have a stake more in the New Orleans musicians than you did in others?
I wasn't really making the distinction yet myself. I was interested in good jazz musicians, and I used a lot of good Chicago and New York musicians.
In other words, you hadn't come to your narrow definition of jazz yet.

That's right. And, for example, many times people worked for me, like Mesro and Pee Wee Russell and Miff Mole and Joe Sullivan. This was all jazz to you? All jazz to me. Still is all jazz. It is? Yes. But anyway, I came to know all these people. Art Hodes used to come and work for me frequently. And it eventually came to a point where I was identified with jazz in Philadelphia, so that nobody even thought of doing anything with jazz in Philadelphia without calling me first.
